title: Two weeks to a roadmap you can actually run.
summary: A focused audit that inventories workflows, scores opportunities by impact, effort, and risk, and produces a sequenced AI roadmap.
audience: Owners and operators who need to decide where AI is worth adopting and what to leave alone.
deliverables: Tooling shortlist with fit and cost notes
timeline: One to three weeks depending on the number of workflows, stakeholders, and whether a proof of concept is included.
fit: Organizations with repeatable workflows and a decision-maker available
Teams seeking a ranked plan rather than another demonstration
Not necessary when the build scope is already validated
evidence: Transparent impact, effort, and risk scoring
methodology: Read out the roadmap and decisions
assumptions: Workflow owners can provide representative examples
A budget owner participates in prioritization
limitations: The sprint is not legal or regulatory advice
Final cost and timing require a scoped agreement

title: Design the workflow before anyone builds it.
summary: A build-ready blueprint defining every AI step, prompt, decision rule, checkpoint, human review, and failure path before implementation.
audience: Teams with one identified process that must be specified rigorously before money goes into a build.
timeline: Scoped to one or several connected workflows and their complexity.
fit: A specific repeatable process is already selected
The team wants edge cases and review designed before implementation
Use strategy first when the priority workflow is still unclear
assumptions: Workflow owners can test the proposed design
Consequential outputs retain accountable human approval
limitations: A blueprint does not by itself implement or operate the system

title: We build the thing, and hand you the keys.
summary: Implementation of a scoped assistant, workflow, or knowledge system, tested on real work and transferred with documentation and operator enablement.
audience: Teams with a validated scope or blueprint that are ready to move from plan to production.
deliverables: Recorded handover and post-launch support window
timeline: Typically staged by scope, beginning with a single assistant or workflow and expanding only after validation.
fit: A design is validated or can be locked quickly
Representative work is available for testing
The team values maintainability and ownership
methodology: Ground the system in authorized material
assumptions: The client can provide authorized systems and source material
An accountable owner accepts the handover
limitations: An off-the-shelf tool may be preferable to a custom build

title: Say yes to AI without saying yes to the exposure.
summary: A practical governance setup defining acceptable use, data handling, disclosure, review, and rollout for teams already adopting AI.
audience: Leaders accountable for confidential, regulated, client-facing, or otherwise consequential work.
timeline: Scoped by team size, industry, current use, and the depth of policy and enablement required.
fit: AI is already being used ahead of formal policy
Sensitive or confidential information is handled
Leadership wants enforceable rules people can follow
methodology: Roll out and maintain the framework
assumptions: Leadership will support and enforce the adopted framework
Qualified counsel addresses jurisdiction-specific legal requirements
limitations: This service supports but does not replace licensed legal, security, privacy, or compliance advice

title: Fluency for the whole team, not just the early adopters.
summary: Live, hands-on training built around the team’s actual work, teaching useful mechanics and the judgment to know when AI should not be used.
audience: Teams with uneven AI adoption that need shared skills and shared safe-use rules.
timeline: A focused session, a multi-session series, or a deeper internal-lead cohort depending on roles and goals.
fit: Teams of roughly five to fifty seeking a common baseline
Leadership wants practice on real work
Tools and an adoption direction are already selected
assumptions: Participants can access approved tools and examples
limitations: Training does not substitute for a strategy, governance program, or technical implementation

title: A senior AI partner, without the full-time hire.
summary: Ongoing strategy, prioritization, implementation support, governance maintenance, and team enablement for organizations treating AI as a durable capability.
audience: Teams with live AI work and no senior internal owner who need continuity across projects.
timeline: Month-to-month cadence scaled from strategic advisory to deeper hands-on involvement.
fit: AI is an ongoing organizational capability
The same partner needs to retain context across initiatives
A single bounded need is better handled as a project
methodology: Report progress, risks, and next decisions
assumptions: The retainer has access to the context needed for decisions
limitations: Fractional leadership does not replace every specialist or executive function
